terms.grammar: verb, first conjugation, transitive: aliquem (sibi fīlium) adoptāre
evidence: Ter. Ad. 47: hunc majōrem adoptāvī mihi
Cic. Brut. 77: quī hunc minōrem Scīpiōnem ā Paulō adoptāvit (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: To take someone in the place of a son or grandson, with ab for the natural father (Lewis & Short). The parent gives a child adoptandum (Ter. Ad. 114); the adopted son is fīlius adoptīvus, and the adoption adoptiō. Its first sense is “choose” (see adopt, take up).

evidence: Cic. Fin. 1.24: ēmancipāre fīlium alicui in adoptiōnem (Lewis & Short, as Fin. 1.7)
Vell. 2.8.2: dare sē alicui in adoptiōnem (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: In Roman law the adoption of a child still in his father’s power; taking in a man already independent was arrogātiō (Lewis & Short). in adoptiōnem dare, give for adoption.
Of the adopted child (fīlius adoptīvus, against nātūrālis) and of the adoptive parent (pater adoptīvus, Dig.); Ovid uses it of a graft on a tree (Ars 2.652).

phrases.latin: uxōrem dūxit; nātī fīliī duo: inde ego hunc majōrem adoptāvī mihi; ēdūxī ā parvulō; habuī, amāvī prō meō
phrases.english: he married; two sons were born; then I adopted the elder one as my own; I brought him up from a little boy; I kept him and loved him as mine

phrases.latin: Tuum fīlium dedistī adoptandum mihi: is meus est factus.
phrases.english: You gave me your son to adopt: he has become mine.

sources: Lewis & Short: adopto · Lewis & Short: adoptio · Lewis & Short: adoptivus
Terence checked against the Perseus Latin texts (11 November 2026).
